questions.question: How do you implement a custom UserDetailsService and UserDetails in Spring Security?
questions.title: UserDetailsService and UserDetails — Custom Implementation
questions.direct_answer: UserDetailsService is a single-method interface that loads user data by username; Spring Security calls it during authentication. UserDetails is an interface describing the loaded user — credentials, account status flags, and granted authorities. You implement both to connect Spring Security to your own database or user store, replacing the default in-memory user management.

interviewer_intent.testing: Whether the candidate can wire Spring Security to a real user database — the most common integration task.
interviewer_intent.common_mistake: Returning a plain Spring Security User object without implementing account expiry or lock flags, causing confusing authentication failures.
interviewer_intent.to_stand_out: Discuss caching UserDetails to avoid database hits on every request, UserDetailsPasswordService for password upgrade, and the difference between isEnabled() and isAccountNonLocked().

sections.title: UserDetailsService Is the Bridge Between Your Database and Spring Security's Authentication Engine
sections.content:
Spring Security doesn't care where your users live — a relational database, LDAP, a REST API, an in-memory map. It only needs one thing: a `UserDetailsService` that takes a username string and returns a `UserDetails` object. **Your entire user model gets filtered through this one-method interface.**

The `UserDetails` contract carries everything Spring Security needs: username, hashed password, four account-status booleans, and a collection of `GrantedAuthority` objects representing roles and permissions. `DaoAuthenticationProvider` calls `loadUserByUsername()`, receives the `UserDetails`, and then uses `PasswordEncoder` to verify the submitted password against the stored hash.

The relationship between `UserDetailsService` and your domain model is intentional separation. Spring Security's authentication engine never sees your `User` entity directly — it sees only `UserDetails`. This means you can evolve your domain model without breaking authentication, and you can provide exactly the subset of user data that authentication needs.

The common mistake surfaces weeks into a project: developers implement the minimum (username, password, one role) and hardcode the four status booleans to return `true`. Later, when the product needs account lockout or forced password expiration, those hardcoded returns mean the security flags do nothing — the column exists in the database, but `isAccountNonLocked()` always returns `true` regardless. **Map these flags to real entity fields from the start**, even if you initialize them all to `true` in the initial migration.

sections.title: The Four Status Flags That Cause Silent Authentication Failures
Connecting UserDetailsService to Spring Security — The ROLE_ Prefix and Correct Wiring
Caching UserDetails and UserDetailsPasswordService — Production-Level Optimizations
Key Points
sections.content:
- **`UserDetailsService.loadUserByUsername()` is called on every request when session-based auth is used** — cache the result with `@Cacheable` or in a Redis session to avoid a database query per request.
- **`UserDetails` interface requires `isAccountNonExpired`, `isAccountNonLocked`, `isCredentialsNonExpired`, `isEnabled`** — returning `true` for all four accepts every user; returning `false` for any one causes `DisabledException` or `LockedException`.
- **`UsernameNotFoundException` should not distinguish 'user not found' from 'wrong password'** — throwing `UsernameNotFoundException` with a different message for each case leaks username enumeration information to attackers.
- **`UserDetailsPasswordService` supports automatic password rehashing** — implement it to upgrade BCrypt work factor on next login without requiring users to reset passwords.
- **`DaoAuthenticationProvider` can be replaced** — implement `AuthenticationProvider` for OAuth2 tokens, LDAP, SAML, or API key authentication; multiple providers are tried in order by `ProviderManager`.

questions.question: What are the trade-offs between session-based and token-based authentication in Spring Security?
questions.title: Session-Based vs Token-Based Authentication
questions.direct_answer: Session-based authentication stores user state server-side in a session tied to a cookie, making revocation instant but requiring sticky sessions or a shared session store in clustered deployments. Token-based authentication (typically JWT) is stateless — all user data is encoded in the token — which scales horizontally with no shared state, but revocation is difficult until the token expires. The right choice depends on scalability requirements and how critical immediate revocation is.

interviewer_intent.testing: Whether the candidate understands stateful vs stateless architecture trade-offs, not just syntax.
interviewer_intent.common_mistake: Claiming JWTs are always better — missing that revocation, token size, and secret management are real drawbacks.
interviewer_intent.to_stand_out: Discuss opaque tokens with an introspection endpoint as a middle ground, or refresh token rotation as a revocation strategy.

sections.title: JWTs Aren't Always Better — Revocation and Token Size Are Real Problems You'll Hit in Production
sections.content:
Developers default to JWTs because "stateless is better." The missing nuance: stateless means the server **cannot invalidate a token until it expires.** If a user's account is compromised, you cannot force logout — the JWT remains valid until its expiry, potentially for hours or days. Implementing a token blocklist to solve this reintroduces server-side state, which negates much of the stateless advantage. You've now built a worse session system.

Session-based authentication stores only a session ID in the cookie (32 bytes). The server holds the session data — or a shared store like Redis does. The server has full control: `session.invalidate()` immediately renders the session ID useless. The trade-off is that **sessions require coordination** in clustered deployments — either sticky sessions (routing all requests from a user to the same server) or a shared session store (adding a network round-trip per request).

Token-based authentication (JWT) embeds claims in the token itself and sends it on every request. The server validates the signature without server-side storage — no database lookup, no Redis round-trip. The token is self-contained. The real trade-offs that tutorials skip: **JWTs are large** (a typical JWT with roles is 800+ bytes; a session ID is 32 bytes), the payload is encoded (not encrypted, anyone with the token can read the claims), and they can't be revoked.

The choice should follow the architecture. Single-server web app with a database? Sessions are simpler and correct. Microservices where each service independently validates tokens? JWT or opaque tokens with introspection. The trend toward JWT is driven by microservices architectures — not by JWT being inherently superior.

sections.title: Sessions vs JWTs — Every Trade-off That Matters in Production
sections.content:
Neither approach is universally correct. The trade-offs are genuine.

| Aspect | Session-Based | Token-Based (JWT) |
|---|---|---|
| **State location** | Server-side (memory or Redis) | Client-side (inside the token) |
| **Scaling** | Requires sticky sessions or shared store | Stateless — any server validates |
| **Revocation** | Instant — `session.invalidate()` | Not possible without a blocklist |
| **Token size** | 32-byte session ID cookie | 800+ bytes per request |
| **Secret management** | Session store access credentials | Signing key (symmetric or key pair) |
| **XSS risk** | Low — cookie with HttpOnly/Secure | High if stored in localStorage |
| **CSRF risk** | Yes — cookies sent automatically | No — Authorization header requires JS |
| **Cross-domain** | Difficult — cookie domain restrictions | Easy — Authorization header works anywhere |
| **Best for** | Web apps, admin panels, monoliths | APIs, microservices, mobile clients |
| **Spring config** | Default — `SessionCreationPolicy.IF_REQUIRED` | `SessionCreationPolicy.STATELESS` |

**The 401 vs 403 distinction disappears** when JWTs expire — an expired token produces 401 (unauthenticated) even if the user's account is active. This is expected but surprises developers who test with long-lived tokens in development and see different behavior in production.

**CSRF and sessions together:** if you store a JWT in a cookie instead of the `Authorization` header, you gain the HttpOnly security benefit but reintroduce CSRF risk — the cookie is sent automatically by the browser. Spring Security's CSRF protection must be re-enabled in this case.

sections.title: Opaque Tokens and Refresh Rotation — When You Need Revocation Without Server-Side Sessions
sections.content:
Sessions and JWTs represent opposite ends of the revocation spectrum. **Opaque tokens** occupy the middle ground that most tutorials ignore.

An opaque token is a random string with no embedded claims — it looks like a session ID. When a resource server receives an opaque token, it sends it to the authorization server's introspection endpoint, which validates the token and returns the associated claims. Revoking an opaque token means marking it invalid at the authorization server — the next introspection call reflects that immediately. This gives you JWT-like stateless APIs (no shared session store between services) with session-like revocation (instant, at the authorization server).

The cost is a network call per authenticated request. Caching introspection responses for 30–60 seconds reduces load while maintaining near-real-time revocation. This is the pattern services like Stripe and Twilio use — tokens are opaque to callers, the authorization server validates them with full revocation support.

**Refresh token rotation** is the practical revocation mechanism within the JWT model. Access tokens expire in 15–30 minutes (short enough that a stolen token has limited window). Refresh tokens are longer-lived but rotate on each use — a new refresh token is issued every time the old one is used. If an attacker steals a refresh token and uses it, the legitimate user's next refresh attempt uses the now-invalidated token, and the server detects the reuse. This is automatic compromise detection with no blocklist needed.

My recommendation: use sessions for web applications where server control matters; use JWTs with short expiry and refresh rotation for APIs; consider opaque tokens when you're running an OAuth2 authorization server that needs API-level revocation control.

sections.title: Key Points
sections.content:
- **Sessions are server-side state; tokens are client-side state** — sessions require shared storage (Redis) in multi-instance deployments; tokens (JWT) are self-contained and require no server state.
- **JWTs cannot be revoked before expiry without a blocklist** — a stolen JWT is valid until its `exp` claim; implement a Redis blocklist of revoked token IDs to enable logout and revocation.
- **JWT payload is base64-encoded, not encrypted** — anyone can decode the payload without the signing key; never put passwords, PII, or sensitive data in JWT claims.
- **Opaque tokens with introspection are a middle ground** — the token is a random string stored in Redis; every request introspects it (one Redis lookup per request); revocable without a blocklist.
- **`SameSite=Strict` on session cookies prevents CSRF without CSRF tokens** — modern browsers refuse to send `SameSite=Strict` cookies on cross-origin requests, eliminating the attack vector.

sections.title: How to Answer This Verbally
sections.content:
Session-based and token-based authentication have fundamentally different scaling and revocation characteristics. Choosing between them is an architectural decision, not just a library choice.

**Session-based (stateful)**
- User logs in; server creates a session and stores it (in memory or Redis); client gets a session cookie
- On each request, the server looks up the session in storage to authenticate
- Revocation is instant — delete the session from storage
- Requires sticky sessions or shared storage (Redis) in multi-instance deployments

**JWT-based (stateless)**
- User logs in; server issues a signed JWT; client stores it and sends it in `Authorization: Bearer` header
- On each request, the server verifies the signature — no storage lookup
- Scales horizontally with no shared state between instances
- Revocation requires a blocklist (Redis set of revoked JTI claims) — adds a storage lookup per request

**The JWT payload is not secret**
- Base64 decoding reveals the payload — it is signed, not encrypted
- Do not put sensitive data in claims; use a separate endpoint to fetch user details if needed

**Opaque tokens**
- Random string stored server-side (Redis); each request exchanges it for user data via introspection
- Instantly revocable; one Redis lookup per request — the performance trade-off between sessions and JWTs

questions.question: How should passwords be stored, and what are the differences between BCrypt and Argon2?
questions.title: Password Hashing — BCrypt vs Argon2
questions.direct_answer: Passwords must never be stored in plaintext or with reversible encryption — only one-way adaptive hashing functions designed for passwords should be used. BCrypt is the widely-deployed standard with a configurable cost factor; Argon2 is the 2015 Password Hashing Competition winner with better resistance to GPU and memory attacks. Spring Security's PasswordEncoder abstraction supports both.

interviewer_intent.testing: Whether the candidate understands why general-purpose hash functions (MD5, SHA-256) are inappropriate for passwords and what makes a password hashing function secure.
interviewer_intent.common_mistake: Suggesting SHA-256 with a salt as sufficient for password storage — it is orders of magnitude faster than BCrypt and vulnerable to GPU attacks.
interviewer_intent.to_stand_out: Mention the importance of cost factor tuning to target ~100ms hash time, how DelegatingPasswordEncoder handles algorithm migration, and the risk of pepper vs salt.

sections.title: SHA-256 With a Salt Is Not Password Hashing — It's Fast Enough to Crack Billions Per Second
sections.content:
The fundamental problem with using SHA-256, MD5, or any general-purpose hash function for password storage is **speed**. SHA-256 was designed to hash data as fast as possible — a modern GPU can compute billions of SHA-256 hashes per second. An attacker who steals a database of SHA-256-hashed passwords can test billions of password guesses per second against each hash. Salting prevents rainbow table lookups (pre-computed hash tables) but doesn't slow down brute force at all — the attacker adds the known salt to each guess and hashes at full GPU speed.

**Password hashing functions are intentionally slow.** BCrypt, Argon2, and scrypt are designed to consume configurable amounts of time and resources per hash, making brute force computationally impractical regardless of hardware. BCrypt takes ~100ms per hash with appropriate settings — a billion times slower than SHA-256. An attacker who steals a BCrypt database needs 100ms per guess per GPU, making even a modest offline attack impractically expensive.

Spring Security's `DelegatingPasswordEncoder` solves the migration problem: it encodes the algorithm identifier in the hash string (`{bcrypt}$2a$...` or `{argon2}$argon2id$...`). The application can accept passwords hashed with multiple algorithms simultaneously — users with old BCrypt hashes continue to authenticate while new passwords use Argon2. **When a user logs in with a BCrypt hash and Argon2 is the current default**, `UserDetailsPasswordService.updatePassword()` re-hashes with Argon2 and updates the database — lazy migration on login, no bulk migration or forced password reset needed.

sections.title: BCrypt vs Argon2 — Speed, Memory Hardness, and GPU Resistance
sections.content:
The security advantage of Argon2 over BCrypt is memory-hardness — GPUs can't parallelize memory-intensive operations the way they parallelize compute-intensive ones.

| Aspect | BCrypt | Argon2id |
|---|---|---|
| **Year** | 1999 | 2015 (PHC winner) |
| **Cost dimensions** | Time only (work factor, 2^N iterations) | Time + Memory + Parallelism |
| **Memory hardness** | None | Yes — configurable RAM per hash |
| **GPU resistance** | Moderate | High — GPU parallelism limited by RAM bandwidth |
| **Password length** | Max 72 bytes (silent truncation) | No practical limit |
| **Spring class** | `BCryptPasswordEncoder` (default) | `Argon2PasswordEncoder` |
| **NIST recommendation** | Acceptable | Preferred (SP 800-63B) |
| **Encoding prefix** | `{bcrypt}` | `{argon2}` |

**BCrypt's 72-byte limit** is a subtle security concern: passwords longer than 72 characters are silently truncated before hashing. A password of 73 characters hashes identically to the same first 72 characters with any suffix appended — meaning two different long passwords can be equivalent under BCrypt. For applications that allow passphrases longer than 72 characters, Argon2 or a pre-hashing approach (using SHA-256 to compress the password to 32 bytes before BCrypt) is necessary.

Argon2id's memory cost (recommended: 64MB or more) is what makes GPU attacks impractical. A GPU with thousands of compute cores but shared memory bandwidth can't parallelize Argon2id effectively — each parallel hash attempt requires 64MB of RAM, and the aggregate RAM bandwidth becomes the bottleneck rather than compute throughput. An attacker with ten GPUs gains ten times the compute but cannot overcome the memory bottleneck at scale.

sections.title: Cost Factor Tuning and Lazy Migration With DelegatingPasswordEncoder
Argon2 vs BCrypt in 2024 — When to Upgrade and How to Migrate Existing Password Hashes
sections.content:
BCrypt dominated password hashing for 20 years. Argon2 won the 2015 Password Hashing Competition and is the current academic recommendation. Understanding the difference demonstrates current security awareness.

**BCrypt's limitation:** its cost factor only scales time, not memory. GPU-based password crackers can parallelize BCrypt efficiently across thousands of cores. With modern GPUs, cracking BCrypt at cost factor 10 takes milliseconds per guess in a distributed setup.

**Argon2** introduces a **memory parameter** that makes GPU cracking economically impractical. Argon2id (the recommended variant) requires gigabytes of RAM per operation — scaling this to millions of parallel GPU threads is prohibitively expensive. The three tuning parameters: `memory` (amount of RAM), `iterations` (time cost), and `parallelism` (number of concurrent lanes).

Spring Security supports both: `new BCryptPasswordEncoder(12)` for BCrypt, `Argon2PasswordEncoder.defaultsForSpringSecurity_v5_8()` for Argon2. Both are compatible with Spring's `DelegatingPasswordEncoder`, which prefixes hashes with the algorithm identifier (`{bcrypt}...`, `{argon2}...`).

**Migration without forcing users to re-enter passwords** — the standard approach: at login, after successfully validating the current hash, check if the stored hash uses the old algorithm, and if so, re-hash the password with the new algorithm and update the database. The user logs in normally; the upgrade is transparent. After migration completes, disable the old algorithm.

In practice, BCrypt at cost factor 12-14 remains acceptable for most applications — the switch to Argon2 is a security-depth improvement, not an urgent vulnerability. Prioritize Argon2 for new applications; migration for existing ones can be planned without emergency timelines.

sections.title: Key Points
sections.content:
- **Never use MD5, SHA-1, or SHA-256 for passwords — they are fast by design** — a GPU can compute 10+ billion SHA-256 hashes per second; BCrypt/Argon2 are deliberately slow.
- **BCrypt work factor 10-12 is the current standard; tune to ~100ms on your hardware** — `new BCryptPasswordEncoder(12)` applies 2^12 iterations; increasing by 1 doubles computation time.
- **Argon2id is the OWASP-recommended algorithm as of 2023** — resistant to GPU and side-channel attacks; three parameters: memory, iterations, parallelism; `Argon2PasswordEncoder` is available in Spring Security.
- **`DelegatingPasswordEncoder` supports algorithm migration** — stores `{bcrypt}hash` or `{argon2}hash` in the database; new passwords use the current algorithm; old passwords are verified by their algorithm and re-encoded on next login.
- **`PasswordEncoderFactories.createDelegatingPasswordEncoder()` is the Spring Boot default** — always use a `PasswordEncoder` bean; never call `encode()` without one.

sections.title: How to Answer This Verbally
sections.content:
Password hashing is not encryption — you cannot decrypt it. The goal is to make brute-force attacks computationally impractical. Fast hash functions (MD5, SHA-256) are entirely the wrong tool for this job.

**Why fast hashes fail for passwords**
- SHA-256: a consumer GPU computes ~10 billion hashes per second
- An 8-character password has ~200 trillion combinations — crackable in hours with a dictionary attack on SHA-256
- BCrypt with work factor 12: ~100ms per hash → 10 hashes per second per GPU → decades for the same search space

**BCrypt**
- Work factor (`cost`) is configurable: `new BCryptPasswordEncoder(12)`
- Each increment doubles computation time — tune to ~100ms on your server hardware
- Includes a random salt automatically — no two BCrypt hashes of the same password are identical

**Argon2id — the modern choice**
- Winner of the Password Hashing Competition (2015); OWASP recommendation
- Resists GPU attacks via memory-hardness (memory-intensive algorithm)
- Three tuning parameters: memory (64MB+), iterations, parallelism

**Migration without breaking logins**
- `DelegatingPasswordEncoder` prefixes the hash with the algorithm: `{bcrypt}$2a$12$...`
- Existing BCrypt passwords verify correctly; new passwords are hashed with Argon2
- On next login of an old-hash user, re-encode with the new algorithm and update the stored hash
